Text:
The 5 sections of a CHART narrative are:
{{c1::Chief complaint::C}}
{{c1::History and physical examination::H}}
{{c1::Assessment::A}}
{{c1::Treatment (Rx)::R}}
{{c1::Transport::T}}
Back Extra:
Why: the R comes from Rx, the medical abbreviation for treatment.

Distinguish: CHART's strength is grouping care into small, logical sections that are easy to search; its weakness is being somewhat difficult to learn.
coverage_notes: Grouped first-letter acronym card for CHART.

Text: The two most common narrative formats used in health care documentation are {{c1::CHART}} and {{c1::SOAP}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: CHART = Chief complaint, History and physical exam, Assessment, Treatment (Rx), Transport; SOAP = Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.

Distinguish: CHART groups care into logical, searchable sections but is somewhat difficult to learn; SOAP is fairly simple to learn.
coverage_notes: The two-most-common-formats fact, grouped c1 pair.

Text:
The Transport section of a CHART narrative documents 5 things:
{{c1::how the patient was moved to the ambulance (and possibly why)}}
{{c1::how the patient was transported (positioned and secured)}}
{{c1::whether lights and sirens were used}}
{{c1::where the patient was taken (including room number)}}
{{c1::who received the report and care}}
Back Extra:
Cue: Transport is the final section of a CHART narrative, so the story ends with the hand-off.

Ex: "Moved by stair chair (narrow stairwell), secured supine to the stretcher; transported without lights or sirens; delivered to Room 12; report given to nurse Jones."
coverage_notes: Grouped cohesive list of the T-section's 5 documented items.

Text:
The 4 sections of a SOAP narrative are:
{{c1::Subjective::S}} = {{c2::information from the patient or others on scene}}
{{c1::Objective::O}} = {{c2::findings you gather by examining and measuring the patient}}
{{c1::Assessment::A}} = {{c2::your summary of key findings and impression of the problem}}
{{c1::Plan::P}} = {{c2::the treatment provided}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: Subjective is what you are told (complaint, events, history); Objective is what you measure or observe (vitals, exam findings).

Why: SOAP is fairly simple to learn, and a finished SOAP narrative lets the reader review the assessment and management.
coverage_notes: Rule 0 synthesis of the four adjacent single-word highlights: one grouped two-way card.

Text:
In a SOAP narrative, classify where each item is documented:
The patient describes his pain as "sharp and burning" = {{c1::Subjective::S/O/A/P}}
The respiratory rate you counted during your exam = {{c1::Objective::S/O/A/P}}
Back Extra:
Why: what the patient tells you is Subjective; what you observe, count, or measure is Objective.

Pitfall: a patient's wording stays Subjective no matter how clinical it sounds; it becomes Objective only once you measure it yourself.
coverage_notes: Application card 1 with fresh exemplars per check 16.

Text:
In a SOAP narrative, classify where each item is documented:
Your impression that the patient is likely having an allergic reaction = {{c1::Assessment::S/O/A/P}}
Assisting the patient with his prescribed inhaler = {{c1::Plan::S/O/A/P}}
Back Extra:
Why: Assessment holds your impression of what the problem might be; Plan holds the treatment actually provided.

Pitfall: an impression is written as a possibility ("possible allergic reaction"), not as a settled diagnosis.
coverage_notes: Application card 2 with fresh exemplars per check 16.

Text: The narrative portion of a patient care report (PCR) can be written by following each step of {{c1::the assessment(s) you performed}} as its guideline.
Back Extra:
Cue: the narrative then mirrors the call — standard precautions, scene safety, NOI/MOI, general impression, LOC, chief complaint, interventions, vitals, medical direction, receiving facility, transfer of care.

Ex: interventions are charted with the time completed and the patient's response — "Assisted ventilations with O2 (15 L/min) at 20 BPM with no change in LOC."
coverage_notes: Concept card for the assessment-based narrative approach. Judge: flagged for the dose-class numerics (15 L/min, 20 BPM) in the Ex line — verified verbatim against the page 403 render, but numbers go to Parker regardless.

Text: In a PCR narrative's chief complaint, pertinent patient and bystander statements are recorded {{c1::as direct quotes::how}}, including any pertinent {{c1::denials}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Patient denies chest pain..."

Why: quoting preserves the patient's exact words instead of your paraphrase of them.
coverage_notes: Distinctive-row card: quoted statements including denials.

Text: The number of patients is recorded in a PCR narrative only when {{c1::more than one}} patient is present.
Back Extra: Ex: "This is patient 2 of 3."
coverage_notes: Distinctive-row negation card.

Text: For orders received from medical control, a PCR narrative records 2 things: {{c1::the order as a direct quote}} and {{c1::who gave the order}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: three things get quoted in a narrative — pertinent patient/bystander statements, pertinent SAMPLE/OPQRST answers, and medical control orders.

Ex: "Med control (Dr. Smith): 'Assist the patient with one nitroglycerin tablet.'"
coverage_notes: Distinctive-row card: quoted orders + who gave them.

Text: For the receiving facility, a PCR narrative documents 3 things: {{c1::the facility name}}, {{c1::the area where the patient was delivered}}, and {{c1::the room number (if known)}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: transfer of care is documented separately — the staff member who took over and the time.

Ex: "Delivered to the ED at Memorial Hospital, Room 6."
coverage_notes: Distinctive-row card: destination detail.

Text: At transfer of care, a PCR narrative records 2 things: {{c1::who received your report and took over care (by name)}} and {{c1::the time}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the receiving-facility entry covers the place (facility name, area, room); transfer of care covers the person and the time.

Ex: "Report given to RN J. Smith at 1432."
coverage_notes: Distinctive-row card: named staff person + time; adds the TIME element the CHART Transport card does not test.

Text: {{c1::Medicare and Medicaid::payers}} will reimburse for ambulance transport only if the services are documented as being {{c2::medically necessary}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: medically necessary = it would have been unsafe or impossible to transport the patient by any other means.

Cue: signatures from the patient or guardian are another essential element for reimbursement.

Ex: strong necessity documentation includes the dispatch-reported condition, the condition actually found on scene, treatments with the patient's response, and an objective report of appearance and mental status.
coverage_notes: Reimbursement rule verified verbatim on the page 405 render; consolidation added the on-page Meaning line defining medically necessary (prerequisite closure).

Text:
9 scenarios establish medical necessity for ambulance transport:
{{c1::emergency transport when no other means was possible}}
{{c1::restraint needed to prevent injury to self or others}}
{{c1::oxygen or other emergency treatment required during transport}}
{{c1::unconscious or in shock}}
{{c1::signs of acute respiratory or cardiac distress (shortness of breath, chest pain)}}
{{c1::signs suggesting possible acute stroke}}
{{c1::immobility required for an unstabilized or possible fracture}}
{{c1::severe hemorrhage}}
{{c1::bed-confined before and after the trip}}
Back Extra:
Why: Medicare and Medicaid reimburse ambulance transport only when documentation shows the trip was medically necessary.

Pitfall: necessity also applies to the level of care — documenting ALS interventions for a patient who did not need them is inappropriate.
coverage_notes: Genuine cohesive list kept whole per Parker's preference. Consolidation: unflagged — the page 405 render confirms exactly 9 bullets ending at bed-confined (check 17 satisfied against the full source page).

Text: For ambulance reimbursement, a patient is bed-confined only if 3 criteria are all met: unable to {{c1::get up from bed without assistance}}, unable to {{c1::ambulate}}, and unable to {{c1::sit in a chair or wheelchair}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: bed-confined status counts toward medical necessity only when it applies before and after the ambulance trip.

Distinguish: needing help to walk is not enough — a patient who can sit in a wheelchair is not bed-confined.
coverage_notes: Grouped triple; wording verified complete on the page 405 render.

Text: Even when a patient refuses care, completing a PCR is {{c1::still required::still required/not required}}.
Back Extra: Why: the refusal record must show the patient was competent, was informed of the risks, and was offered care.
coverage_notes: Binary with mandatory forced-choice hint.

Text:
A refusal-of-care PCR documents 4 things:
{{c1::the advice you gave about the risks of refusing}}
{{c1::clinical evidence of competency (such as LOC)}}
{{c1::pertinent patient comments and any advice from the physician/medical control}}
{{c1::a description of the care you wished to provide}}
Back Extra:
Why: the record must prove the refusal was informed and made by someone competent to refuse.

Cue: physician/medical control advice to the patient counts even when given by phone or radio — capture it.
coverage_notes: Grouped cohesive list of the 4 documentation contents.

Text: A car-crash patient with neck pain accepts treatment and transport but refuses a cervical collar. Provide {{c1::all other medical care (including oxygen)}} and document {{c1::the specific refusal (collar declined)}}.
Back Extra:
Why: refusal of care pertains not only to transport — a patient may refuse one aspect of care while accepting the rest.

Pitfall: a collar refusal is no reason to deny oxygen; one refusal never cancels the rest of the care plan.
coverage_notes: Scenario card using the source's own c-collar/oxygen example.

Text: A {{c1::base station}} is any radio hardware containing {{c2::a transmitter::unit}} and {{c2::a receiver::unit}} that is located {{c3::in a fixed place::location}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a mobile radio is installed in a vehicle and a portable radio is handheld — the base station is the one that never moves.

Meaning: a transmitter and a receiver together make up a two-way radio; some base stations have more than one of each.

Ex: dispatch centers, fire stations, ambulance bases, and hospitals often serve as base stations.
coverage_notes: Two-way definition; transmitter+receiver grouped under c2, fixed-place discriminator c3.

Text: Most VHF mobile radios operate {{c1::between 30 and 300 MHz::range}}, whereas UHF mobile radios operate {{c1::between 300 MHz and 3,000 MHz::range}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: VHF = very high frequency; UHF = ultra-high frequency.

Cue: radios operating at 800 MHz, increasingly common in EMS systems, sit in the UHF band.
coverage_notes: Grouped two-sided numeric contrast; flagged for the MHz ranges.

Text: A {{c1::mobile radio::radio type}} is installed {{c2::in a vehicle::where}} and usually operates at {{c3::lower::higher/lower}} power than a base station.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a portable radio is handheld and carried on your person; a base station stays at a fixed site — the mobile radio is the vehicle-mounted middle tier.

Cue: transmission range steps down the same ladder — base station, then mobile, then portable.
coverage_notes: Mobile-radio definition from grounded context; power direction forced-choice.

Text: Communications from a mobile radio are typically limited to {{c1::10 to 15 miles::range}} over average terrain.
Back Extra:
Why: mobile antennas sit much closer to the ground than base station antennas, so mobile signals cannot carry as far.

Distinguish: a handheld portable radio (1 to 5 watts) is even more limited — its antenna stands no taller than the EMT holding it.
coverage_notes: Numeric range card; flagged (10-15 miles, 1-5 watts).

Text: A {{c1::repeater}} is a special {{c3::base station::radio class}} radio that receives messages on one frequency and then automatically {{c2::retransmits them on a second frequency}}.
Back Extra:
Why: base-station hardware brings a large antenna and high power, so a weak signal from a distant portable gets picked up and rebroadcast at full strength.

Ex: two portable or mobile units too far apart to reach each other directly can still communicate by going through the repeater.

Cue: EMS systems built on repeaters usually enjoy outstanding systemwide communications.
coverage_notes: Definition with three clozed facts: name, base-station classification, second-frequency mechanic.

Text: With {{c1::telemetry::transmission process}}, electronic signals are converted into {{c2::coded, audible signals::signal form}} that can be sent by radio or telephone.
Back Extra:
Pathway: coded signals travel by radio or telephone → a decoder at the hospital converts them back into electronic impulses → the impulses are displayed on a screen or printed.

Ex: telemetry is what allows an ECG to be transmitted from the field to the hospital.
coverage_notes: Two-way definition with decode pathway.

Text: A cellular telephone is effectively a {{c1::low-power portable radio::device class}} that communicates through a series of {{c2::interconnected repeater stations}} called cells.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a satellite phone (satphone) uses a satellite instead of a cell to receive and relay its signals.

Ex: EMTs commonly reach receiving facilities by cellular telephone; the cells are linked by a sophisticated computer system and connected to the telephone network.
coverage_notes: Cell-phone-as-radio identity card; satphone contrast.

Text: A {{c1::scanner}} is a radio receiver that searches across several frequencies, stops whenever it receives a broadcast on one, and continues once the message is complete.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: scanners put EMS radio traffic in public ears — always respect patient privacy and speak professionally every time you transmit.

Distinguish: cellular and satellite phones are more private than most radio, but their digital signals make eavesdropping difficult, not impossible.
coverage_notes: One-way describe-to-name definition (meaning side decodable from the term).

Text:
EMS radio transmission modes and the capability that defines each:

Simplex — {{c1::one direction at a time (push to talk, release to listen)}}

Duplex — {{c1::talking and listening at the same time}}

Multiplex — {{c1::two or more frequencies}} carrying {{c1::more than one transmission at once}}, with {{c1::audio and data on separate channels}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: simplex (common on VHF equipment) — while one party transmits, the other can only receive and must wait to reply; duplex (used on UHF frequencies and cellular telephones) — sometimes described as a pair of frequencies; multiplex — the only one of the three that moves voice and data together.

Cue: simplex = one path at a time; duplex = two directions at once; multiplex = many signals at once.
coverage_notes: Rule 0 grouped three-way contrast of the transmission modes.

Text: A paramedic on scene transmits a patient's ECG to the hospital while simultaneously talking with medical control. Transmission mode required? {{c1::Multiplex::simplex/duplex/multiplex}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: duplex covers talking and listening at once, but only multiplex adds data on a separate channel alongside the audio.

Why: the ECG rides a data channel while the voice report rides an audio channel — two or more frequencies working as one system.
coverage_notes: Application card for the duplex-vs-multiplex discrimination; grounded ECG exemplar kept off the grouped card.

Text: Many VHF and UHF channels, commonly called {{c1::MED channels}}, are reserved {{c2::exclusively for EMS use::how}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: hundreds of commercial, local government, and fire service frequencies are also used for EMS communications — MED channels are the dedicated set, not the only set.
coverage_notes: Name + exclusivity fact.

Text: A {{c1::trunking::system type}}, or {{c1::800-MHz::frequency band}}, system assigns {{c2::many (rather than one or two)::how many}} frequencies to a group, and {{c3::a computer}} picks {{c3::the next open frequency}} as each conversation begins.
Back Extra:
Why: constant computer monitoring of frequency load lets the same pool carry far greater traffic — what once needed 30 separate frequencies can run on fewer than 10.

Pitfall: you will likely be on a different frequency each time you key up, and the switch happens without you being aware of it.
coverage_notes: Trunking mechanics; flagged for 800 MHz and the 30-vs-10 frequencies detail.

Text: An {{c1::interoperable::system type}} communications system allows {{c2::all agencies involved::who}} to share information {{c3::in real time::when}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: a voice-over-Internet protocol (VoIP) format connects landlines, cell phones, and computers into one seamless, reliable exchange.

Why: large-scale emergencies pull in law enforcement, fire, and EMS — often across more than one jurisdiction — and every agency needs the same information at the same moment.
coverage_notes: Definition with who/when clozed; VoIP plumbing in Back Extra.

Text: A {{c1::mobile data terminal (MDT)::equipment}} is a small computer terminal inside the ambulance or other vehicle that {{c2::directly receives data from the dispatch center}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a mobile radio in the same vehicle carries voice traffic — the MDT handles the data side of the run.

Why: MDTs give a crew greatly expanded communication capabilities.
coverage_notes: Two-way definition, figure reference stripped.

Text:
When you are on scene, hearing the dispatcher or hospital clearly does {{c1::not::does/does not}} mean you will be heard or understood when you transmit.

Two-way reach is limited by how well {{c1::the weaker radio (yours)::which radio}} can talk back.
Back Extra:
Why: base and repeater stations have higher antennas and much greater power than mobile or portable units, so their signals carry much farther than yours.

Cue: on scene your radio has strong ears but a weak voice — it hears the powerful station far better than it can answer back.
coverage_notes: Asymmetry + limiting principle under one cloze.

Text: {{c1::Paging::alerting method}} is the use of a {{c2::coded tone or digital radio signal}} and a {{c2::voice or display}} message to alert on-duty and off-duty EMS personnel.
Back Extra:
Ex: receivers are pagers (beepers) and desktop monitor radios, usually silent until their specific paging code comes through.

Distinguish: a page may target specific personnel or be a blanket signal that activates every pager in the service.

Why: a page is only the alert — personnel then contact the dispatcher to confirm the message and get the details of their assignment.
coverage_notes: Two-way definition; 'pagers' kept off the visible c1 side.

Text:
Across the 6 phases of an EMS call, a unit typically radios dispatch to:
Initial receipt of call (2) → {{c1::acknowledge the call}}; {{c1::confirm the unit is en route}}
En route (2) → request {{c1::assistance with directions}} or {{c1::additional resources}}, when needed
On scene (4) → {{c1::report arrival at the scene}}; {{c1::check in periodically as a safety measure}}; {{c1::request additional resources}} when needed; {{c1::report leaving the scene}}
Arrival at hospital or point of transfer (1) → {{c1::notify dispatch of arrival}}
Return to service (1) → notify dispatch when {{c1::the unit is available for another call}}
Miscellaneous (1) → notify dispatch (in some systems) anytime the unit is {{c1::not in station}}
Back Extra:
Ex: an arrival report can add obvious size-up details — 'BLS Unit Two is on scene at 3010 Mitchell Street. It is a blue house with a long driveway' — which helps additional units still responding.

Why: dispatchers field hundreds of calls per hour, so transmit only the important information and keep the channel clear.

Pitfall: problems that arise during the response are also reported to the dispatcher as they happen.
coverage_notes: Grouped phase-by-phase dispatch card; folds the two highlighted duties (confirm en route, report arrival) as rows. The 10-20 minute number is externalized to the sibling numeric card.

Text: As an on-scene safety measure, how often will many EMS systems require a unit to transmit a check-in to dispatch? {{c1::Every 10-20 minutes::interval}}
Back Extra:
Why: the scheduled transmission is a safety measure — it confirms to dispatch that the crew on scene is still safe.

Pitfall: not universal — whether and how often to check in varies by EMS system, so follow local protocol.
coverage_notes: Dedicated numeric interval card; flagged per the numeric rule.

Text: When initiating an EMS radio call, address the {{c1::unit you are calling::called unit / your unit}} first, and then provide the name of {{c1::your own unit::called unit / your unit}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: 'Dispatch, this is BLS Unit Two' — name whom you are calling, then who you are.

Pitfall: after the initial call, wait — the unit you called will signal when you can begin the transmission.
coverage_notes: Call-initiation order with forced-choice hints.

Text: When transmitting a number over the EMS radio, such as an address, give both {{c1::the whole number}} and {{c1::its individual digits}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: 'Respond to 1381, 1-3-8-1, Main Street.'

Why: giving the number two ways lets the receiver verify it — one form checks the other.
coverage_notes: Both forms grouped under one c1; source example in Back Extra.

Text: Over the EMS radio, confirm or deny with the words {{c1::'affirmative' and 'negative'::2 words}} rather than the plain everyday words.
Back Extra:
Ex: 'affirmative' in place of yes, 'negative' in place of no — 'Is the scene safe?' 'Affirmative.'

Cue: part of clear-text discipline — plain English, no codes, no slang, no filler such as 'be advised.'
coverage_notes: Radio diction rule; yes/no kept off the visible stem.

Text:
An EMT's radio patient report commonly includes 10 elements, in order:
1. {{c1::Unit ID and service level}}
2. {{c1::Any special alert}}
3. {{c1::Receiving hospital and ETA}}
4. {{c1::Patient's age and sex}}
5. {{c1::Chief complaint and severity}}
6. {{c1::Brief history of current problem}}
7. {{c1::Brief report of physical findings}}
8. {{c1::Summary of care given}}
9. {{c1::Patient's response to treatment}}
10. {{c1::Any additional questions or orders}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the report tells the call's story in order — who we are → any alert → where we're headed and when → who the patient is → what's wrong → how it happened → what we found → what we did → how they responded → what else do you need?

Distinguish: element 8 is the care you gave; element 9 is how the patient responded to that care.

Ex: 'Columbus Fire 2-BLS' (element 1); severe trauma → 'trauma alert', heart attack → 'cardiac alert' (element 2); physical findings cover level of consciousness, general appearance, pertinent abnormalities, and vital signs (element 7).
coverage_notes: All 10 elements verified in order against the page 434-435 renders; one grouped ordered card covering both highlighted marker elements.

Text: In the radio patient report, describe the patient by age and sex; the patient's {{c1::name::identifier}} is never given over the air.
Back Extra:
Why: the airwaves are public and scanners are popular — a broadcast name can be overheard, a violation of the patient's privacy.

Pitfall: the same public-channel logic demands objective, impartial patient descriptions and zero profanity.
coverage_notes: Negation card on the no-name privacy rule; grounded in the public-airwaves context.
